questiontext.text: Which set contains the three basic pillars of infrastructure?

generalfeedback.text: Compute executes workloads, storage retains data, and networking connects resources. The alternatives describe activities, environments, or application-level concerns rather than the three infrastructure pillars.

answer.text: Deployment, tests, and monitoring
Compute, storage, and networking
Development, test, and production
Applications, users, and code

questiontext.text: Which statement best describes a declarative infrastructure definition?

generalfeedback.text: A declarative definition expresses the intended state. Automation determines the operations needed from the declaration and actual state. Parallel execution may be possible, but it is not what makes a definition declarative, and declarations still have dependencies.

answer.text: It is a script listing commands to run, in the order an administrator would type them.
It specifies the exact sequence of operations needed for each possible starting state.
It describes the desired state, and the tool works out the steps needed to reach it.
It lets the tool run independent changes in parallel, which is what makes it declarative.

questiontext.text: An automation run has successfully reached the desired state. Its inputs and the relevant external state then remain unchanged. What should a second idempotent run do?

generalfeedback.text: Once the desired state is satisfied, repeating an idempotent operation under unchanged relevant conditions should cause no further managed-state changes. Checking the current state is compatible with idempotence; doing nothing without checking does not establish correctness.

answer.text: Check the current state, find nothing to change, and make no changes.
Recreate the resources so the team can show they are still reproducible from the code.
Skip checking the current state, since the previous run already succeeded, and report success.
Add another copy of each declared resource.

questiontext.text: A team moves from managing virtual machines under IaaS to a managed application platform under PaaS. Which responsibility would typically move towards the provider?

generalfeedback.text: PaaS typically transfers more operating-system and runtime-platform maintenance to the provider. The exact boundary depends on the service. The application team still owns its business requirements and application code.

answer.text: Deciding which business requirements the application should meet
Maintaining and reviewing the team's own application source code
Choosing which application features to release and when
Patching and upgrading the operating system and the runtime

questiontext.text: Which pair of benefits best explains how version-controlling infrastructure definitions helps a team deliver changes reliably?

generalfeedback.text: Review and automated checks before application can catch mistakes, for example firewall rules codified in Git and checked by pipeline policies before they reached the devices. The commit history records who changed what, when, and why, and makes rollback possible. Version control alone neither applies changes nor restores deleted data: code lives in Git, and only automation delivers the change. Reviewed changes still need validation.

answer.text: It preserves change history, so reverting a definition also restores any deleted application data.
It gives one shared definition, and storing it in Git keeps the running infrastructure in sync with it.
Changes can be reviewed and checked before they apply, and the history shows who changed what and why.
It makes environment differences visible, so validation is no longer needed once a change is approved.

questiontext.text: Two servers were created from the same definition. An administrator changes a managed setting manually on one server. Which description and response best address the situation?

generalfeedback.text: Drift is a difference between actual managed state and intended state. Investigate it before reconciliation: an unauthorized change may need reversal, while a legitimate change should be reviewed and recorded in the definition. A shared origin does not guarantee continued consistency.

answer.text: The server has drifted; compare it with the definition, then restore the setting or review and update the definition.
The definition is now obsolete; copy the new setting into it and apply it to the other server straight away, without a review.
The servers are still consistent because they came from the same definition, so a note about the manual change in the operations log is enough.
The difference is a fault in the server; rebuild both servers immediately.

name.text: L1 Q7 Mutable and immutable infrastructure

questiontext.text: A server needs an operating-system configuration change and stores application data that must survive the update. Which plan correctly distinguishes mutable and immutable approaches?

generalfeedback.text: Mutable updates change an existing instance. Immutable updates replace it with an instance prepared from the updated definition or image. Persistent application data needs separate storage or a verified transfer/recovery process; infrastructure definitions do not generally contain that data.

answer.text: A mutable update replaces the server; an immutable update modifies the existing server and keeps its identity and data in place.
Both approaches modify the existing server; the immutable one also records the change in version control.
A mutable update changes the existing server; an immutable update replaces it and rebuilds the application data from the infrastructure definition.
A mutable update changes the existing server; an immutable update replaces it and keeps the data in separate storage or migrates it.

name.text: L1 Q8 Separating infrastructure and server configuration

questiontext.text: A deployment needs networks and virtual machines, plus software and service configuration inside those machines. Which organization best separates responsibilities while keeping the deployment coordinated?

generalfeedback.text: Provisioning establishes resources and connectivity; server configuration establishes software, files, and service state. Clear boundaries with explicit information flow support focused review and reuse. Separate repositories are optional and do not by themselves keep dependencies synchronized.

answer.text: Keep a complete, independent copy of the whole setup for each environment, so that a change made for one environment stays out of the others.
Separate provisioning from server configuration, pass the needed resource details between them, and review each part on its own.
Put provisioning and configuration in separate repositories and rely on operators to keep the connection details in sync.
Keep resource provisioning in code, and document the manual software setup as the interface between the two.

name.text: L1 Q9 Dependencies and changing resource information

questiontext.text: An application server requires a network. A later configuration step needs the server's assigned address, which may change when the server is replaced. The team currently copies that address into several files. Which design best preserves both dependency order and current connection information?

generalfeedback.text: Explicit dependencies identify what must exist or be known before another step can proceed. Passing current resource outputs avoids stale, duplicated addresses after replacement. File names alone do not encode those resource relationships, and correct ordering alone does not keep copied values current.

answer.text: Declare the network-to-server and server-to-configuration dependencies, and derive the address from the current server output.
Number the definition files in deployment order, and keep the original address as a default value in each configuration file so it stays available.
Start the stages together, and keep retrying the configuration against the previously recorded address until the server becomes reachable.
Create the network and the server in order, and let each configuration stage keep its own reviewed copy of the address.

name.text: L1 Q10 Shared definitions and environment differences

questiontext.text: Development and production use copied infrastructure definitions. They should share an application structure, but production needs greater capacity. Independent edits have introduced differences whose purpose is unclear. Which approach best preserves legitimate differences and prevents accidental divergence?

generalfeedback.text: A shared definition captures the common structure, while explicit environment values retain intended capacity differences. Compare definitions and actual state with the agreed design, then review and validate changes. Identical values are not required, and undocumented manual exceptions undermine the shared source of truth.

answer.text: Keep the definitions separate and periodically copy production over development, using production capacity as the shared baseline.
Require identical definitions and values in both environments, and record production capacity changes in an operations checklist.
Share the common structure, keep environment-specific values explicit, and review today's differences against the intended design.
Create one shared definition, allow manual environment-specific changes after deployment, and review changes to the shared definition.
